title: Rohatsu 2013
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shares a story about Chiyono, an illiterate servant who learned the importance of cultivating compassion from an elderly nun, illustrating that we can already embody the qualities of a Buddha in our daily lives by acting with kindness and awareness, rather than waiting for some big realization or insight. This teaching encourages us to let go of distinctions between people and simply be present with others, just as it is, finding beauty and interconnectedness in everyday activities. By embracing this approach, we can create an environment where everyone's unique contributions are valued and nurtured, ultimately leading to the unfolding of a shared enlightenment.

sentences.text: Thanks for coming.
Just a visit for the talk.
Sorry, I made you wait a little while in the lobby, I think.
Sorry, it wasn't too cold.
And wonderful, another year of doing our collaborative Rohatsu sesshin, Seattle Bellingham Sanghas, and people from many points in between, and further afield.
So really our question this retreat is how to honor Buddha, right?
How to celebrate what would be a really appropriate and really wholesome way for us to celebrate something called Buddha and awakening, which we don't have a clue what it is.
That's a good challenge.
Maybe we have a little clue, we think.
One of the ways that we celebrate Buddha in the Zen tradition is by following the schedule.
Sometimes they say the schedule is the first teacher.
And I want to beg your forgiveness, I'm not going to follow the schedule at this retreat.
We had our Rohatsu sesshin scheduled long ago, and many Zen groups all over the world do Rohatsu sesshin about this time of year.
The Zen Buddhists decided that Buddha was definitely awakened on the morning of the eighth day of the twelfth month.
At that point it would have been a lunar calendar, and then when Japan adopted the Gregorian calendar, they kept it on December 8th.
So just like we're sure that Christ was born on December 25th.

So there are celebrations all over the world, so that's a fun thing to contemplate, especially maybe in those moments in Zazen that are your least favorite moments in Zazen, you can remind yourself, actually this is helpful, I've done this, that there are people all over the world sitting this very sesshin right now.
Some are already going, some are about to start.
Another one that's about to start on Saturday night is a Rohatsu sesshin in Mexico, at the Mar de Jade retreat center a little bit north of Puerto Vallarta.
And this is taught by Norman Fischer, my teacher, Sangha's guiding teacher.
Anyway, he called me up about three, four months ago and said, can you come help me lead that sesshin?
And I said, no way, we already got our own Rohatsu.
And he said, well, it starts kind of late, it starts on the eighth, or the seventh, I guess, the evening of the seventh.
And I thought about this some more, and maybe this would be a good thing, to help Norman lead a sesshin in Mexico.
And I brought it to our Sangha leaders.
A little bit embarrassed: can I leave early?
It's really sweet actually, they're very supportive, and a nice, really refreshing little bit of indignation too, which I really appreciated.
Which was like, what, you think we can't do this without you?
That was nice for me.
So all this is by way of begging your pardon that I'm going to leave tonight to go to Mexico.
That's why I'm cramming in as much teacher stuff today as we can, doing Dokusan and the talk.
And Jeff also has been very supportive, so I want to thank my teaching partner for taking the load.
And I especially wanted to thank our local Sangha organizers who worked really hard to make this moment possible.
Bob and Kate and Talus principally, so thank you guys.
Somehow Talus is doing this well enough that he actually is making a few appearances in Zendo, so that's pretty good.
Good work.
So I thought we'd start our celebration with a story.
*Chiyono was a servant in a Zen convent who really wanted to practice Zazen.
One day she approached an elderly nun and asked, "I'm only of humble birth.
I can't read or write and must work all the time.
Is there any possibility that I could attain the way of Buddha, even though I have no skills?"
The nun answered her, "That's wonderful, my dear.
In Buddhism there are no distinctions between people.
There is only this.
Each person must hold fast the desire to awaken and cultivate a heart of great compassion.
People are complete as they are.
If you don't fall into delusive thoughts, there is no Buddha and no sentient being.
There is only one complete nature.
If you want to know your true nature, you need to turn towards the source of your delusive thoughts.
This is Zazen."*
Let me read that again.
It's the nun giving her a teaching.
*"How wonderful, my dear.
In Buddhism there is no distinction between people.
There is only this.
Each person must hold fast the desire to awaken and cultivate a heart of great compassion.
People are complete as they are.
If you don't fall into delusive thoughts, there is no Buddha and no sentient being.
There is only one complete nature.
If you want to know your true nature, you need to turn towards the source of your delusive thoughts.
This is called Zazen."* Chiyono, the servant, said with great joy,
*"With this practice as my companion, I only have to go about my daily life, practicing day and night."
After months of wholehearted practice, she went out on a full moon night to draw water from the well.
She put the water in the bucket to see the full moon.
The bottom of her old bucket was only held together by bamboo straps, and at that moment the bottom of the bucket suddenly gave way.
And the reflection of the moon vanished with the water.
When she saw this, she attained a great realization.
Her enlightenment poem was this.*
*With this and that, I tried to keep the bucket together.
And then the bottom fell out.
Where water does not collect, the moon does not dwell.
With this and that, I tried to keep this bucket together.
And the bottom fell out.
Where water does not collect, the moon does not dwell.*
So this, by the way, is a story, one of 100 stories in a very important book we should all get, called The Hidden Lamp: Stories from 25 centuries of awakened women.
Just a little bit of history with that book, but I'll tell you later.
So I was thinking, since it's Rohatsu, again, how do we celebrate Buddha?
How do we really show our appreciation and our gratitude for this possibility?
Do we sit really strongly?
Am I moving an inch?
Are we really precise with the forms?
Keeping the silence scrupulously.
Doing our oryoki practice just so, at least once we know how to do it.
Standing just the right way.
Moving very carefully.
Upright.
Dignified.
Because one way to think of Zen practice is it's actually a ritual.
The whole thing is a ritual enactment of being Buddha.
Of course we don't think that way.
We think, if I just do this, maybe I'll get some result that I want for myself.
If I sit for some years, maybe I'll get some peace.
But another way of looking at practice is that when we're practicing with a good spirit, we already are Buddha.
Just Buddha sitting.
Just Buddha walking.
Just Buddha eating.
Maybe if we really take this on, this being Buddha, we are honoring Buddha.
It's a little different from our cultural frame, where we think this has to be some spontaneous inner thing that we're expressing.
How could this possibly be right?
You just act like Buddha then you're Buddha?
No way.
I'm not worthy.
Fill in the blank.
Is there some big realization we should have?
Something we should figure out and learn in order to honor Buddha?
Some big aha moment.
Some new insight, new perspective about our life.
Is that what we should have or do somehow?
How do we go about doing that anyway?
Is there a skill we need to learn?
Do we need to study lots of obscure religious texts of some kind?
What's interesting about this story is it brings up someone who did not feel skilled, an illiterate woman, working there at the convent.
There are actually many stories in the Zen tradition of people who are not literate or are somehow lower in the caste system in some way.
Maybe we can relate to this regardless of our position in society, which is for the most part pretty good.
We're inside in a warm room and we had food today, so we're already probably at a high percentage.
And yet maybe we don't feel so skilled, so worthy, so complete.
But one of the other things that's interesting about this story is it opens with a woman who doesn't feel too worthy.
And she receives some real loving.
Did you notice that?
The nun did not give her tough love or put her in her place or give her a tough practice to work on.
The nun said, how wonderful.
You can do that.
It doesn't depend on skill.
She's offered a lot of encouragement, loving, support.
And sometimes we think the Zen of these old stories is not loving and warm.
There's whacking with sticks and so on.
Which actually maybe could be loving and warm if you do it right.
But here's a story about two women having a warm, loving interaction and the receiving of this teaching that it's not about skill.
Do we believe that?
It's not about skill.
It's about devotion.
It's about awakening the heart of compassion, it said.
And it's about turning towards those very qualities that maybe are the qualities that are telling us we are unworthy and no good.
Turning towards the source of your delusive thoughts.
Devotion and turning towards difficulty.
Feeling our own suffering.
Feeling the basic human feeling of being a person.
Right here, right now, as we are.
The story doesn't say, but it sounds like Chiyono didn't really change her routine.
She didn't start going to the meditation hall.
She didn't learn special practices or mantras or poems.
What's implied is that she just kept doing the work that she already had been doing.
Cooking, cleaning, hauling water, obviously.
Taking care of the nuns.
But somehow she engaged in her ordinary work from that moment forward.
And she was probably doing this a little bit already, just spontaneously.
But engaged in her ordinary work with a sort of extraordinary spirit.
Saying to herself, with this practice as my companion, my companion, I only have to go about my daily life.
Practicing day and night.
Somehow she worked with her relationship and her attitude to herself in her activity.
And her activity became awakening.
Not just chores.
Somehow she could see more clearly the incredible beauty and richness of the interconnected universe that is right there when you pick up your broom or hold your bowl.
She could feel the moon beams flowing as she swept the floor.
She understood that the wind is listening when she dusts.
And she could see all the people around as Buddha, even with their problems and oddnesses.
I felt this way a little bit at the grocery store a couple days ago.
It had been a pretty stressful week.
My wife is having some health problems and she's stressed out.
So we were doing the grocery shopping together so she'd feel organized before I disappear to Mexico.
Hopefully she's going to join me in Mexico, so it's not too bad.
We'll see.
So anyway, we went to the grocery store.
And one of the things that she does that I don't bother to do is she's very strategic about when she goes to the store, so it won't be too crowded.
She's got some limitations, so she needs to be able to park nearby and so on.
I usually just blow this off and show up when I show up.
And so we ended up at Trader Joe's.
I don't know if you know the Bellingham Trader Joe's, but it's a pretty busy place, always.
We got there during an especially busy time.
The parking lot and all the neighboring streets were full of cars and the place was packed with people.
And how do we usually respond when we enter the store and it's packed with people?
We don't like this, right?
This is bad for me.
Why are these other people impinging on my needs?
Who do they think they are?
I should be able to get smoothly to that shelf right now.
And somehow I didn't go into that.
I started really looking around at the people doing their shopping, like really looking at them.
Not people watching, not trying to analyze the fashion trends or anything, but trying to really see them as human beings.
And somehow it was very different from how I usually experience looking at a bunch of people.
I could see old people and young people.

And it was so apparent in a powerful way, the way the young people were turning into old people right before my eyes. [unclear: "You just look like a young person that's very temperate."] I could somehow feel or imagine.
I think actually there was a mother and daughter together, like a grown daughter.
Somehow that helped me see that.
And then I said, well, that's true for everyone.
Not just an idea, but really a felt experience.
And that the old people were young people just like yesterday.
How quickly the kaleidoscope turns.
And each person part of a bigger family.
I had this really felt sense of each person being connected to who knows how many people.
And they're just there representing a whole network of interconnection.
They're interacting in different ways.
It was really beautiful, actually.
I still got my shopping done.
But it was like a great thing that there were so many people so I could keep practicing this way.
Seeing the uniqueness and the beauty of each person.
And the fragility and temporariness of their position.
An awesome display.
A crowded grocery store in a way is like an awesome display of life.
As is the deep wilderness and trees and all that.
Also awesome.
What popped to my mind was, I don't know if you remember the 1960s movie Harold and Maud.
Remember that movie?
In case you don't know that movie, Harold is a young morose teenager.
And he somehow becomes friends with an older woman who's a very cheerful, jubilant, wise woman.
They should have put Harold and Maud in the book here of koans, actually. [unclear: "Good woman's co-on was one time Harold."] They had been, I think, at a carnival or something.
It was the first time Harold had had a good time, you know, forever.

And he says to her after the carnival, and she'd been interacting with lots of people at the place, like the guy with the stuffed animals, she'd been really having a good time with everybody they met.
And Harold turns to her and says, "How come you get along with people so easily?"
And she just laughs and says, "They're my species!"
Like, why wouldn't you get along with people?
So I don't know if I can quite describe this experience.
And I'm sure you've had your version of this experience too.
Really wonderful moment.
A couple of 10, 20 minutes maybe.
But also really ordinary.
I didn't see special lights or emanations or anything like that.
But I did see something I usually didn't see.
Something beautiful about ordinary people just buying groceries for dinner.
And maybe that's how it was for Chiyono in this story.
As she did her work in the monastery and the convent more and more, the ordinary activities were revealed for their full beauty and majesty and richness.
And finally she went out on a full moon night to get water from the well in her old bucket.
You get a feeling everything was pretty well patched together in this place.
And then pouring water into the bucket with the ladle, she could see the moon, the full moon reflected in the water.
You can imagine it little by little coming into focus.
And it must have been such a beautiful sight.
Have you seen the beautiful crescent moon these last few evenings?
Rising in the evening or setting in the evening.
But then suddenly the bottom of the bucket just falls away.
The moon disappears.
So maybe that's how we can honor the Buddha in our Rohatsu retreat.
Taking really good care of everything we do.
Paying attention to its awesome beauty.
Even the awesome beauty of our delusive thoughts.
Our tightness, you know.
Our resistance.
But don't feel like you have to hold the bottom onto that bucket.
Let the bottom drop out.
Woosh.
Let it all go.
There's nothing to hold onto really.
Nothing to figure out.
Nothing ultimately really that we have to do.
Jeff was saying last night, just to be here is enough.
Just to be together.
Just to love each other.
I have actually many times noticed the awesome beauty of people sitting in meditation.
That's pretty easy to see.
So I hope you'll see that too.
But of course it's true of everything.
That we can support each other in letting the practice be.
Opening the heart of compassion.
For our self, sure.
For everyone here, sure.
For all beings, no difference.
Sooner or later, the bottom of the bucket will drop out.
Don't get out your hammer and try to break the bucket though.
It happens in its own time.
So thank you again for your steady practice.
And I have to now thank you in advance for the rest of your practice.
This retreat.
And I'm sure that the enlightenment ceremony on Sunday morning will be really beautiful.
I'll be thinking of you when you're walking around the block at six in the morning, and it's 25 degrees.
And you're in Mexico.
The low will be 60 and the high 82.
So I'm sure you'll think of me.
So thanks, what a treasure.
I really mean it.
Who would have thought, like I was saying last night, I really mean this, I really like this unbelievable miracle.
That all this could come together somehow.
And it really depends on every one of us to keep unfolding this miracle.
Keep nurturing it and taking care of it.
So every one of us is so important.
We have different roles because that makes the thing work out.
But every one of us is equally important.
Just like Chiyono and the nun.
Each of us creating Buddha's enlightenment over and over.
